title: 22. Interview: SRE Concepts
summary: Interview Q&A for SRE Concepts — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 SRE Concepts interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an SLA, and why must they be ordered correctly?
**Answer:** An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measure of service health — typically a ratio of good events to total events, such as "fraction of HTTP requests returning in under 400 ms with a 2xx status." An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the internal target value for that SLI over a window, like 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the contractual, customer-facing promise, set lower than the SLO (e.g., 99.5%) and accompanied by financial penalties if breached. The ordering matters because the SLO sits above the SLA, creating a safety margin: an internal SLO miss is a leading indicator that, if not corrected, will eventually breach the SLA and trigger refunds or churn. Google's rule of thumb is that the SLA should sit one nine below the SLO. If the SLO equals the SLA, every internal miss is already a customer-visible breach, leaving no room to recover. If the SLA is far below the SLO, customers receive worse service than they paid for, and the team has no signal to invest in reliability.

**Visual:**
```
SLI (measure)  <  SLO (target)  <  SLA (contract)
99.95% actual    99.9% target     99.5% promised
                  |--- margin ---|
                  (room to recover before breach)
```

### Q2. Explain the error budget and how it governs the product-vs-reliability trade-off.
**Answer:** The error budget is the inverse of the SLO expressed as an allowance: for 99.9% availability over 30 days, the budget is 43.2 minutes of allowed unavailability. The budget is a shared resource between product and engineering. While budget remains, product can ship features, push risky migrations, and approve deploy windows; engineering can freeze infrastructure for upgrades. Once the budget is exhausted, engineering gets to gate all further changes behind reliability work — feature deploys freeze, migrations pause, and the team pays down toil until the budget recovers. This converts what was previously a political argument ("when can we ship?") into a quantitative one ("do we have budget?"). The deeper insight is that the budget is replenished only by elapsed time at SLO, so reliability work that prevents future incidents has a direct, measurable effect on shipping velocity. Google's experience is that teams using error budgets ship more features over a year than teams without them, because they spend less time firefighting self-inflicted outages.

**Visual:**
```
SLO 99.9% over 30d  ->  budget = 43.2 min/mo

Budget remaining:   [##########..........]  ship features
Budget exhausted:   [####################]  freeze + pay down toil
Budget recovering:  [####################]  resume carefully
```

### Q3. What is toil, and why does SRE cap it at 50% of each engineer's time?
**Answer:** Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly with service growth — restarting crashed pods, hand-filling capacity tickets, copying log lines into postmortems, manually rotating certificates. SRE caps toil at 50% of each engineer's time for two reasons. First, toil does not compound: an hour spent restarting pods today does not make tomorrow's restarts easier, whereas an hour spent automating the restart eliminates the task permanently. Teams that spend 80% of their time on toil never escape it, because they have no time to build the automation that would free them. Second, toil is demoralizing and burns out engineers — Google's internal data showed that teams above 50% toil had higher attrition and lower incident response quality. The 50% cap is therefore both an engineering principle (compounding work beats linear work) and a human principle (sustainable pace prevents attrition). When a team exceeds 50% toil for two quarters, the response is not to hire more toilers but to stop taking feature work until the highest-toil tasks are automated.

**Visual:**
```
SRE time split (target):
  |----- 50% engineering (automation, design, postmortems) -----|
  |----- 50% toil (ops, paging, tickets) ----------------------|

Toil > 50% for 2 quarters:
  -> freeze feature work
  -> automate top toil item per sprint
  -> re-measure next quarter
```

### Q4. How do you define a good SLI? What separates a useful SLI from a vanity metric?
**Answer:** A useful SLI captures user-visible service health directly. The canonical recipe is "the ratio of good events to total events, where good is defined by what the user experiences as success." For an HTTP API, that means counting as good only requests that returned a 2xx status within a latency threshold (say, 400 ms at p99) — not all 2xx regardless of latency, and not average latency. A vanity metric, by contrast, is something that is easy to measure but does not reflect user experience: average latency (which hides tail latency where users actually suffer), CPU utilization (which is a capacity indicator, not an experience indicator), or "number of requests served" (which counts failed requests the same as successful ones). The discipline is to ask, for each candidate SLI, "if this metric is green, is the user definitely happy?" If the answer is no, the SLI is wrong. Google's SRE workbook specifies that every SLI must be defined by a measurement specification (where, how, over what window) and a threshold specification (what counts as good), so that two engineers reading the SLI agree on its value.

**Visual:**
```
Good SLI:   good = (status 2xx) AND (latency < 400ms)
            total = all requests
            SLI   = good / total   [captures user experience]

Bad SLI:    average latency        [hides p99 tail]
            CPU utilization        [capacity, not experience]
            requests served count  [counts failures as success]
```

### Q5. What is a blameless postmortem, and why is blamelessness an engineering principle rather than a social nicety?
**Answer:** A blameless postmortem is a post-incident review conducted under the assumption that the engineer who triggered the incident did what any reasonable engineer would have done given the information and tools they had. The fault is in the system — the deploy process that allowed the bad config, the access controls that allowed the destructive query, the test suite that did not catch the broken code — not the engineer. Blamelessness is an engineering principle, not a social nicety, because blameful postmortems produce bad engineering outcomes: they cause engineers to hide future incidents, which prevents learning, which guarantees recurrence. The engineer who triggered the incident is the most important person in the postmortem room because they know more about what happened than anyone else; if they are afraid of being blamed, they will withhold information, and the postmortem will be wrong. Etsy, Google, and Netflix all codify this in writing: postmortems focus on systemic causes, action items address systemic weaknesses, and the engineer's name appears only as a contributor to the document, never as the cause of the incident. The result is faster learning, lower recurrence, and higher engineering quality.

**Visual:**
```
Blameful:   "Alice pushed the bad config"  -> next time, Alice hides it
Blameless:  "The deploy process allowed an unreviewed config"
              -> action item: require config review
              -> Alice contributes her full knowledge of what happened
```

### Q6. What is the role of capacity planning in SRE, and how does it differ from reactive scaling?
**Answer:** Capacity planning is the discipline of forecasting future resource needs (CPU, memory, disk, network, CDN) 6–12 months ahead and converting the forecast into a procurement plan. It treats capacity as a known function of traffic growth, per-request cost, and required failure headroom (typically N+1 or N+2 to survive a single-region or single-zone failure). Reactive scaling, by contrast, waits for capacity pressure (high CPU, queue depth) and then adds capacity — this works for elastic cloud resources but fails for resources with long lead times (bare-metal orders take 6–12 weeks, cross-region bandwidth contracts take months) and for resources that fail catastrophically when over-subscribed (a saturated database does not degrade gracefully, it falls over). SRE's discipline is to forecast monthly, plan for peak × (1 + margin), and provision ahead of need. Google's Search capacity plan uses Monte Carlo simulation over traffic distributions and failure modes to produce probabilistic headroom targets; smaller teams use simpler deterministic models, but the principle — capacity is forecastable, not reactive — is universal.

**Visual:**
```
Reactive:    CPU>80% -> add node (works for cloud, fails for bare metal)
SRE plan:    forecast traffic * per-req cost * (1 + N+2 margin)
             -> order ahead of need, never run < 30% headroom

12-mo forecast:  Q1 100 pods, Q2 140, Q3 200, Q4 280
                 -> order bare metal in Q2 for Q3 arrival (8-wk lead)
```

### Q7. What is change management in the SRE sense, and why is progressive delivery its core technique?
**Answer:** Change management in SRE is the set of practices that reduce the rate at which changes (deploys, config edits, migrations) cause incidents — Google's data shows roughly 70% of outages are caused by changes, not by capacity or dependency failures. The core technique is progressive delivery: ship a change to a small subset first (canary or ring 0), observe error rate and latency, then expand to 1%, 10%, and 100% only if metrics stay green. The supporting techniques are reversibility (every deploy must have a one-command rollback) and change isolation (never change code and config simultaneously, so a regression's cause is unambiguous). Microsoft Azure's "Safe Deployment" formalizes this as ring-based rollout (ring 0 = team, ring 1 = internal, ring 2 = early adopters, ring 3 = production) with automated rollback on error-rate threshold. Netflix's Chap, Spinnaker, Flagger, and Argo Rollouts all encode the same principle: ship small, ship slowly, ship reversibly. The trade-off is deployment velocity (progressive delivery is slower than push-to-prod) versus incident rate (progressive delivery catches regressions before they affect all users).

**Visual:**
```
Progressive delivery rings:

ring 0: team         [deploy] --watch 5m--> ok?
ring 1: internal     [10k users] --watch 30m--> ok?
ring 2: early adopters [10% prod] --watch 2h--> ok?
ring 3: production   [100% prod]

If error_rate > threshold at any ring -> auto-rollback
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your service has an SLO of 99.9% over 30 days. After a bad deploy, you burned 12 minutes of the 43.2-minute budget in one hour. What do you do?
**Answer:** 12 minutes of budget in 1 hour is a burn rate of 8.64× sustainable (sustainable would be 43.2 min / 720 h = 0.06 min/h; you burned 12, so burn = 12/0.06 ≈ 200× for that hour — actually let me recompute properly). The correct framing is: a 14× burn over 1 hour consumes 2% of the 30-day budget in that hour, which means an SLO breach in 5 hours if sustained. 12 minutes in 1 hour is roughly 14× burn (since 1 hour = 1/720 of the window, and 12 minutes = 12/43.2 = 27.8% of budget in 1/720 of the window, which is 200× — extremely high). Immediate action: roll back the deploy (one command, since every deploy must be reversible) and confirm the error rate drops to zero. If rollback is not possible, route traffic to the previous version via the load balancer. Open a SEV-2 incident, page the on-call if not already paged, and freeze all further changes to this service. Within 24 hours, run a blameless postmortem to identify the systemic cause (deploy gate failed? canary did not catch it? test gap?) and produce action items. With 31 minutes of budget remaining, the service can absorb one more small incident this month but must run cleanly for the rest of the window or the SLO will breach.

**Visual:**
```
Budget: 43.2 min/30d.  Used: 12 min in 1h.  Remaining: 31.2 min.
Burn rate: 200x sustainable  -> SEV-2, page on-call
1. Rollback deploy (1 command)
2. Confirm error rate -> 0
3. Open incident, freeze further changes
4. Blameless postmortem within 24h
5. Action items: fix deploy gate / canary / tests
```

### Q2. Product wants to ship a major feature on Friday. Your error budget is at 20% remaining. How do you respond?
**Answer:** The error budget answer is quantitative, not political: with 20% remaining, the team has roughly 8.6 minutes of unavailability left this window. A Friday deploy of a major feature carries elevated risk because (a) traffic patterns over the weekend differ from weekday patterns, so canary signals are noisier; (b) the on-call team may be thinner over the weekend, slowing response; (c) any incident that occurs Friday evening will not be investigated until Monday, extending time-to-resolve. SRE's posture is that budget remaining is permission to ship, but the team should spend it deliberately: ship Tuesday or Wednesday instead, when traffic is normal and the team is fresh, so that any regression is caught within hours rather than days. If product insists, the compromise is to ship behind a feature flag (off by default), enable for 1% of traffic Friday, monitor over the weekend, and ramp to 100% Monday morning. The deeper lesson is that error budgets do not eliminate judgment — they give the team a quantitative basis for the conversation, and Friday-afternoon deploys remain a known anti-pattern even when budget exists.

**Visual:**
```
Budget: 20% remaining (8.6 min)
Friday major deploy risk:
  - weekend traffic patterns (noisier canary)
  - thinner on-call (slower response)
  - incident investigates Monday (slow resolve)

Compromise: ship behind flag, 1% Friday, 100% Monday
```

### Q3. Your team's on-call rotation is buried in pages — 200 pages per week per engineer. How do you apply SRE principles to fix this?
**Answer:** 200 pages per week per engineer is roughly 28 pages per day, which is catastrophic: the engineer cannot do engineering work, is heading for burnout, and the pages themselves are losing signal (a page that fires 28 times a day is not actionable). The SRE playbook is alert hygiene plus toil elimination. First, audit every alert for actionability: an alert that fires and the on-call engineer immediately acknowledges without action is noise — disable it or convert it to a dashboard. Second, deduplicate: many alerts fire on the same underlying cause (a slow dependency triggers latency alerts on five services); consolidate to a single symptom-based alert. Third, tune thresholds to burn-rate-based multi-window alerts (14× over 1h pages, 6× over 6h tickets) so that only sustained breaches page. Fourth, every page must have a runbook link — if the on-call does not know what to do, the alert is incomplete. Fifth, track "alert fatigue" as a metric (pages per on-call shift) and set a target (Google's target is <5 pages per 12-hour shift). Sixth, the alerts that survive this audit each represent a toil item — automate the response so the alert never needs to fire again. After one quarter of this discipline, page volume typically drops 80–90%.

**Visual:**
```
Before: 200 pages/wk/engineer (28/day, no engineering time)
Audit pass:
  1. disable alerts that fire but no action taken
  2. dedupe multi-service alerts -> one symptom alert
  3. burn-rate thresholds (14x page, 6x ticket)
  4. every page -> runbook link
  5. track pages/shift, target <5/12h
  6. automate the response of each surviving alert
After: ~20 pages/wk/engineer, 80-90% reduction
```

### Q4. Your CTO asks why the team spends 50% of its time on "engineering" instead of running the service. How do you justify the SRE time split?
**Answer:** The justification is compounding returns. Toil — manual operational work — does not compound: an hour spent restarting pods today does not make tomorrow's restarts easier, and the team will spend the same hour next week. Engineering work — automation, design, postmortems — compounds: an hour spent automating the restart eliminates the task permanently, freeing that hour every week forever. Over a year, a team that spends 50% of time on engineering eliminates 26 toil items and builds a library of reusable automation; a team that spends 100% on toil has the same toil next year plus whatever new services were added. The CTO's framing implicitly assumes that "running the service" is the work, but SRE's framing is that "running the service" should be a shrinking fraction of the work as the platform matures. Google's data: SRE teams that hit the 50/50 split ship more features over a year than teams that operate at 80% toil, because they spend less time firefighting self-inflicted outages. The 50% engineering time is not overhead; it is the mechanism by which operations scales sublinearly with traffic.

**Visual:**
```
Toil (linear):     hour today -> hour next week -> hour next year
Engineering (compounding): hour today -> 0 hours next week -> 0 hours forever

Year 1:  50% engineering -> 26 toil items automated
Year 2:  same team, 2x services, same on-call load
         (toil-free platform scales sublinearly)
```

### Q5. A mid-deploy incident reveals your deploy process has no automatic rollback. The CTO wants a fix this quarter. What do you build?
**Answer:** The fix is a reversible deploy pipeline with automated rollback on error-rate threshold. Step one: make every deploy versioned and atomic — the previous version must remain available (container image, binary, config snapshot) so rollback is `kubectl rollout undo` or `deploy --previous`, not a rebuild. Step two: instrument a rollback trigger — a metric query (e.g., `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[2m]) > 0.01 * rate(http_requests_total[2m])` for 2% 5xx rate) that fires automated rollback within 60 seconds of detection. Step three: use progressive delivery (canary 1% → 10% → 100% with a 5-minute hold at each step) so the rollback fires before the change reaches all users. Step four: add a manual `rollback` command as a one-liner for the on-call engineer, with a clear audit log of who rolled back and when. Step five: require every change to pass a "reversibility review" — if the change cannot be rolled back (e.g., a database migration that drops a column), it must be split into a reversible sequence (add new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old column — each step reversible). Microsoft Azure, Netflix Chap, and Spinnaker all encode this; the open-source equivalents are Flagger and Argo Rollouts.

**Visual:**
```
Deploy pipeline:
  build v2  ->  canary 1% (5m hold, watch 5xx rate)
            ->  10% (5m hold)
            ->  100%

  if 5xx > 2% for 60s at any step:
     auto-rollback to v1 (one command, <60s)

  manual: `deploy rollback <svc>` (audited)

  irreversible changes (drop column):
     split -> add col / dual-write / backfill / switch / drop
     (each step reversible, deploy over a week)
```

### Q6. Your team is debating whether to set the SLO at 99.9% or 99.99%. What factors should drive the decision?
**Answer:** The decision is driven by user expectation, cost, and the marginal value of each nine. First, user expectation: if the service is a consumer-facing API where a 0.1% failure rate is invisible (most users retry and succeed), 99.9% is fine; if it is a payment or auth service where every failure is a customer-visible error, 99.99% may be required. Second, cost: each additional nine costs roughly 10× in engineering and infrastructure (the "rule of nines"). Going from 99.9% (43 min/mo budget) to 99.99% (4.3 min/mo) eliminates the budget for any planned downtime, requires multi-region active-active (a single region's failure must not breach the SLO), forces canary-based deploys everywhere, and demands automated rollback within seconds. Third, marginal value: 99.9% to 99.99% reduces user-visible failures by 10×, but the next nine (99.999%, 26 sec/mo) reduces by another 10× at another 10× cost — diminishing returns set in quickly for most services. Google's rule: set the SLO at the level users notice, plus one nine of headroom below the SLA. Netflix targets 99.99% for playback start (every failure is visible) but 99.9% for recommendation refresh (failures are invisible).

**Visual:**
```
9s    budget/mo   cost        typical use
99    432 min     1x          internal tools
99.9  43.2 min    10x         consumer APIs
99.99 4.3 min     100x        payment, auth, playback
99.999 26 sec    1000x        only safety-critical

Rule: set SLO where users notice + 1 nine below SLA
```

### Q7. You join a startup with no SLOs, no error budgets, and a culture of "ship fast, fix later." How do you introduce SRE practices without killing velocity?
**Answer:** The trick is to introduce SRE practices as enablers of velocity, not constraints on it, and to start with the highest-leverage, lowest-friction practices first. Step one: instrument the service with the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) on a single dashboard — this takes a week and immediately makes deploys safer because regressions are visible. Step two: define one SLI and one SLO for the most user-visible service (e.g., login or checkout) at a level you are already meeting — do not set an aspirational SLO that will fail on day one. Step three: introduce error budgets as a vocabulary, not a gate — for the first quarter, just compute and publish the budget burn weekly so the team sees the correlation between risky deploys and budget loss. Step four: automate the single most painful toil item (usually deploys or rollback) so the team experiences the compounding benefit of engineering time. Step five: run blameless postmortems on the next incident — the cultural win of blamelessness is immediate and converts skeptics. Step six: only after these are in place, start using the error budget as a deploy gate. The pattern is: measure → publish → improve → constrain. Skip any step and the team will experience SRE as bureaucracy.

**Visual:**
```
Q1: instrument + dashboard (1 wk, immediate value)
Q2: define SLO you already meet + publish budget weekly
Q3: automate top toil item (deploys or rollback)
Q4: blameless postmortems on every incident
Q5: budget as deploy gate (now the team trusts it)

Pattern: measure -> publish -> improve -> constrain
(skip any step = team experiences SRE as bureaucracy)
```
